title: Programming Foundations
content: Software engineering is the disciplined creation of reliable, maintainable software. Programming is instructing a computer via code. KEY CONCEPTS: Variables, data types, control flow (if/loops), functions, data structures (arrays, objects). Syntax vs logic. WORKED EXAMPLE: A function that takes inputs, processes them, returns output — the building block of all software. PRACTICE: 1) Write pseudocode for a login check. 2) List 4 data types. 3) Explain a loop's purpose.
quiz_json: [{"q": "What is the primary purpose of programming?", "options": ["To instruct a computer via code", "To design hardware components", "To manage software licenses", "To create graphic designs"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "Programming involves writing code to instruct a computer on what tasks to perform."}, {"q": "Which of the following is NOT considered a key concept in programming foundations?", "options": ["Variables", "Control flow", "Networking protocols", "Functions"], "correct": 2, "explanation": "Networking protocols are not part of the basic programming concepts like variables, control flow, and functions."}, {"q": "What is the difference between syntax and logic in programming?", "options": ["Syntax is the structure of code; logic is the correctness of the program's behavior", "Syntax is about program behavior; logic is about code appearance", "Syntax refers to hardware; logic refers to software", "Syntax and logic mean the same thing"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "Syntax refers to the rules and structure of the code, while logic refers to whether the program behaves correctly and produces the intended results."}]

title: Data Structures & Algorithms
content: Data structures organize data; algorithms process it efficiently. KEY CONCEPTS: Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash maps, trees, graphs. Big-O notation (time/space complexity). Sorting and searching. WORKED EXAMPLE: A hash map gives O(1) lookup vs O(n) for scanning an array. PRACTICE: 1) Match a structure to a use case. 2) Explain O(n) vs O(1). 3) Describe when to use a tree.
quiz_json: [{"q": "Which data structure provides O(1) average time complexity for lookup operations?", "options": ["Hash map", "Array", "Linked list", "Stack"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "Hash maps use hashing to provide average O(1) time complexity for lookups, unlike arrays or linked lists which require scanning."}, {"q": "What is the main difference between O(n) and O(1) time complexity?", "options": ["O(n) scales linearly with input size; O(1) is constant time", "O(1) scales linearly; O(n) is constant", "Both scale linearly", "Both are constant time"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "O(n) means the time grows linearly with input size, while O(1) means the time is constant regardless of input size."}, {"q": "When is it most appropriate to use a tree data structure?", "options": ["To represent hierarchical relationships", "To implement a queue", "For constant time lookup", "To store unordered key-value pairs"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "Trees are ideal for representing hierarchical data, such as file systems or organizational charts."}]

title: Software Design & Architecture
content: Good architecture makes software maintainable and scalable. KEY CONCEPTS: Separation of concerns, modularity, design patterns (MVC, singleton, factory), SOLID principles, coupling vs cohesion. WORKED EXAMPLE: MVC separates data (model), display (view), and logic (controller) so each changes independently. PRACTICE: 1) Explain separation of concerns. 2) Name a design pattern's use. 3) Define loose coupling.
quiz_json: [{"q": "Which design principle emphasizes dividing a software system into distinct sections, each handling a separate concern?", "options": ["Separation of concerns", "Coupling", "Cohesion", "Singleton pattern"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "Separation of concerns refers to dividing a system into parts that each address a separate concern, improving maintainability and scalability."}, {"q": "In the MVC design pattern, what is the primary responsibility of the Controller?", "options": ["Manage data and business logic", "Display the user interface", "Handle user input and update the model/view", "Ensure only one instance of a class exists"], "correct": 2, "explanation": "The Controller handles user input and updates the Model and View accordingly, separating logic from data and display."}, {"q": "What does 'loose coupling' in software architecture mean?", "options": ["Modules depend heavily on each other", "Modules have minimal dependencies on each other", "Modules are tightly integrated", "Modules are combined into a single unit"], "correct": 1, "explanation": "Loose coupling means modules have minimal dependencies, allowing them to change independently and improving flexibility."}]

title: Web & Systems
content: Modern software runs across clients, servers, databases, and networks. KEY CONCEPTS: Frontend vs backend, APIs (REST/GraphQL), HTTP, databases (SQL/NoSQL), client-server model, statelessness. WORKED EXAMPLE: A browser (client) calls a REST API (server) that queries a database and returns JSON. PRACTICE: 1) Trace a web request end-to-end. 2) Compare SQL vs NoSQL. 3) Define an API endpoint.
quiz_json: [{"q": "Which of the following best describes the role of a frontend in modern web applications?", "options": ["It handles user interface and client-side interactions", "It manages database queries and storage", "It routes network traffic between servers", "It processes server-side business logic"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "The frontend is responsible for the user interface and client-side interactions, running in the user's browser or device."}, {"q": "What is a key difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?", "options": ["SQL databases are stateless; NoSQL databases are stateful", "SQL databases use structured schemas; NoSQL databases are schema-less or flexible", "SQL databases only support REST APIs; NoSQL only supports GraphQL", "SQL databases run on clients; NoSQL databases run on servers"], "correct": 1, "explanation": "SQL databases use structured schemas with tables and relations, while NoSQL databases are schema-less or have flexible schemas, allowing for more varied data models."}, {"q": "In the client-server model, what does it mean that HTTP is stateless?", "options": ["Each request from client to server is independent and does not retain session information", "The server maintains user session data between requests", "Clients must store all data locally without server communication", "HTTP automatically manages user authentication across requests"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "HTTP being stateless means each request is independent; the server does not retain any session information between requests unless additional mechanisms are used."}]

title: Version Control & Collaboration
content: Teams build software with version control and disciplined workflows. KEY CONCEPTS: Git (commits, branches, merges), pull requests, code review, CI/CD (automated testing/deployment). WORKED EXAMPLE: A feature branch is developed, reviewed via PR, tested by CI, then merged and auto-deployed. PRACTICE: 1) Explain branching. 2) Describe a code review's value. 3) Define CI/CD.
quiz_json: [{"q": "What is the primary purpose of creating branches in Git?", "options": ["To isolate feature development from the main codebase", "To delete old code versions", "To speed up the deployment process", "To automatically review code"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "Branches allow developers to work on features or fixes separately without affecting the main codebase until changes are ready to be merged."}, {"q": "Which of the following best describes the value of a code review in a pull request?", "options": ["It automatically deploys code to production", "It helps catch bugs and improve code quality through peer feedback", "It merges branches without conflicts", "It runs automated tests on the code"], "correct": 1, "explanation": "Code reviews provide an opportunity for team members to examine changes, suggest improvements, and ensure code quality before merging."}, {"q": "What does CI/CD stand for and what is its main benefit?", "options": ["Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment; automates testing and deployment", "Code Inspection/Code Documentation; improves code readability", "Centralized Integration/Centralized Delivery; manages team communication", "Continuous Improvement/Continuous Design; enhances software architecture"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "CI/CD automates the process of testing and deploying code changes, enabling faster and more reliable software delivery."}]

title: Quality, Testing & Security
content: Reliable software requires testing and security discipline. KEY CONCEPTS: Unit/integration/end-to-end tests, TDD, debugging, secure coding (input validation, auth, encryption), OWASP top risks. WORKED EXAMPLE: Validating and sanitizing user input prevents injection attacks. PRACTICE: 1) Name 3 test types. 2) Explain input validation. 3) Describe TDD.
quiz_json: [{"q": "Which of the following is NOT a common type of software test?", "options": ["Unit test", "Integration test", "End-to-end test", "Performance tuning"], "correct": 3, "explanation": "Unit, integration, and end-to-end tests are common testing types. Performance tuning is an optimization activity, not a test type."}, {"q": "What is the primary purpose of input validation in secure coding?", "options": ["To improve application speed", "To prevent injection attacks", "To enhance user interface design", "To increase code complexity"], "correct": 1, "explanation": "Input validation ensures that user inputs are checked and sanitized to prevent injection attacks and other security vulnerabilities."}, {"q": "In Test-Driven Development (TDD), what is the correct sequence of steps?", "options": ["Write code, write tests, refactor", "Write tests, write code, refactor", "Refactor, write code, write tests", "Write code, refactor, write tests"], "correct": 1, "explanation": "TDD follows the cycle: write a failing test first, then write code to pass the test, and finally refactor the code."}]

title: Grandmaster — Scalable Systems
content: Building for scale requires distributed systems thinking. KEY CONCEPTS: Load balancing, caching, database sharding, microservices, message queues, eventual consistency, the CAP theorem. WORKED EXAMPLE: A high-traffic app caches hot data and shards its database to handle millions of users. PRACTICE: 1) Explain caching's benefit. 2) Define microservices. 3) Describe the CAP tradeoff.
quiz_json: [{"q": "What is the primary purpose of load balancing in scalable systems?", "options": ["To distribute incoming network traffic across multiple servers", "To store frequently accessed data for faster retrieval", "To divide a database into smaller, manageable pieces", "To ensure data consistency across distributed nodes"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "Load balancing distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers to prevent any single server from becoming a bottleneck, improving system availability and scalability."}, {"q": "Which of the following best describes microservices architecture?", "options": ["A single monolithic application handling all functions", "A system where services are tightly coupled and share a database", "An approach where an application is composed of small, independent services", "A method of caching data to reduce database load"], "correct": 2, "explanation": "Microservices architecture breaks an application into small, independent services that can be developed, deployed, and scaled independently."}, {"q": "According to the CAP theorem, which three properties cannot be guaranteed simultaneously in a distributed system?", "options": ["Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance", "Caching, Availability, Performance", "Consistency, Atomicity, Partition tolerance", "Load balancing, Availability, Partition tolerance"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "The CAP theorem states that in the presence of a network partition, a distributed system can guarantee either consistency or availability, but not both simultaneously."}]

title: King Level — Engineering Leadership
content: At King level you architect systems and lead engineering at scale. KEY CONCEPTS: System design at scale, technical strategy, tradeoff analysis, mentoring, building engineering cultures, choosing what NOT to build. WORKED EXAMPLE: A staff engineer designs a platform others build on, multiplying the whole team's output. PRACTICE: 1) Design a system for 10M users. 2) Make a build-vs-buy call. 3) Define engineering leverage.
quiz_json: [{"q": "What is a key responsibility of an engineering leader at the King level?", "options": ["Designing systems at scale", "Writing all the code themselves", "Managing only small teams", "Focusing solely on individual tasks"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "At the King level, engineering leaders architect systems and lead engineering efforts at scale, focusing on system design and strategy rather than just individual contributions."}, {"q": "Which of the following best describes a critical tradeoff an engineering leader must consider?", "options": ["Choosing what NOT to build", "Writing detailed documentation", "Attending all meetings", "Coding every feature personally"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "A King level leader must strategically decide what NOT to build to focus resources effectively and maximize impact."}, {"q": "How does a staff engineer at King level multiply the team's output?", "options": ["By designing platforms others build on", "By working longer hours", "By micromanaging the team", "By avoiding mentoring"], "correct": 0, "explanation": "By designing scalable platforms that others build on, a staff engineer amplifies the productivity and impact of the entire engineering team."}]
